[2026-08-04, round 2] I did a targeted follow-up on the 'Captain John Spotswood Jones (1740-1797)' lead this round and found nothing under that exact name-and-dates combination -- the Bedford County, Virginia will index for 1754-1830 has zero entries for any John Jones or Spotswood Jones. I'm treating this specific name-and-dates combination as unverified and probably a conflation, not deleting it as a lead, but downgrading it significantly. What I think actually happened: there IS a real, well-documented Captain John Spotswood (c.1748-1801) of the 10th Virginia Regiment -- a Spotswood, not a Jones -- who was wounded at both Brandywine and Germantown. Those are the SAME two battles that show up in Gray's account of our Llewellen Jones's own service. I think someone along the way merged this real Spotswood soldier's battle record with our Jones family, creating the 'John Spotswood Jones' hybrid name. Here's what I think is actually documented and real: Gray's article says Llewellen Jones's father was 'Captain John Jones of the 6th Virginia Regiment' -- just John Jones, no Spotswood middle name, no Bedford County, no 1740/1797 dates. I found genuine documentary support for the STRUCTURE of Gray's lineage claim (that 'another granddaughter' of Orlando Jones married a Captain John Jones): a real 1771 York County, Virginia deed names 'John Jones and Frances Barber, his wife,' and Frances Barber Jones is documented as Orlando Jones's granddaughter in the published Rowland Jones genealogy (https://archive.org/download/jstor-1914886/1914886_djvu.txt). So the lineage STRUCTURE Gray describes checks out against an independent primary source, even though the specific 'Spotswood' name and 1740-1797 dates don't check out.

column11: If Columbus and Reuben Jones were born enslaved at Avalon, their later purchase of pieces of that same land, and eventual service in the Alabama legislature, can be read as an act of reclamation -- taking hold of the ground that once held them in bondage rather than migrating away, as many freedpeople did during Reconstruction. Read this way, their documented choices become an assertion of permanence and belonging against a system built to deny them both. This is an interpretive frame drawn from their documented actions (land purchase, continued residence, public office), not a claim to any specific quoted intention by either brother -- no first-person statement from Columbus or Reuben has been located.

column4: The 1820 Alabama legislative manumission act (Acts, Nov. 1820, p.62, approved Dec. 11, 1820; DB1 row 176) authorized John N.S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones to emancipate 'a mulatto woman, named Elizabeth age forty years; a mulatto girl, named Ann, aged 6; a mulatto girl, named Evelina, 13; and a mulatto child, named Shandy, 3 years old.' Shandy's age (3 in Dec. 1820) matches Shandy Wesley Jones's well-documented birth date of Dec. 20, 1816 in Huntsville, Madison Co., AL. All independent sources agree: born enslaved in Huntsville/Madison Co. AL 1816, emancipated as a young child, moved to Tuscaloosa before age 21, married Evalina Love in 1837, became a prosperous barber and real estate investor, served in the Alabama House of Representatives 1868-1870 (Tuscaloosa's first Black elected official), fled KKK violence to Moundville then Mobile in 1871, appointed to U.S. Customs House by President Grant, pastored Little Zion/Big Zion AME Zion Church, died Feb. 4, 1886, buried Magnolia Cemetery Mobile. The O'Rourke Family Tree's placement of him as a child of Llewellen Jones and 'Elizabeth (slave)' matches this exactly.

column11: No first-person account from Shandy Wesley Jones describing his infancy at Avalon has been located in this research. His documented trajectory -- freed at age three alongside his mother and sisters, raised to literacy at a time when teaching a Black child to read was itself an act of resistance, and eventually seated in the Alabama legislature -- invites, without proving, a narrative of a mother who used the narrow freedom granted in 1820 to build toward possibilities direct enslavement would have foreclosed. The 'incestuous relationship' paternity claim reported by Mobile Bay Magazine, if accurate, is also a reminder of how routinely archives of slavery elide or euphemize coercion within enslaving households; this project treats that gap itself as evidence of erasure, not merely a missing biographical detail.

column11: Mary Ann "Polly" Jones's recorded lifespan -- born enslaved in Alabama in 1830, dying free in Powhatan County, Virginia in 1893 -- spans the entire arc from slavery through emancipation to old age as a free woman, yet no document reviewed so far preserves her own words about that journey. One might imagine her leaving Alabama sometime after 1865, whether to reunite with family, to escape the same land and community that had once enslaved her mother Penny and held her own childhood, or simply following economic opportunity available to freedpeople willing to relocate. This is an interpretive frame offered to make her sixty-three years of life feel like more than two dates on a family tree; it is not a documented account of her motives or experiences, which remain to be found.

I also want to pin down: is Llewellen Jones's migration a documented instance of the Broad River Group pattern specifically (i.e., part of the actual Virginia-via-Petersburg-Georgia planter network), or was he merely contemporaneous with that group -- arriving at the same 1809 Huntsville land sale without being a formal member of the network itself?
column3: LeRoy Pope; Thomas Bibb; William Wyatt Bibb; John Williams Walker; Charles Tait; Henry Chambers; Llewellen Jones; John Nelson Spotswood Jones; Alexander P. Jones; Planters and Merchants Bank of Huntsville; Madison County AL 1809 land sale
column4: Secondary source (Huntsville History Collection article, already in DB1 rows 55/169) states Llewellen Jones "came to north Alabama at about the same time as" the Broad River Group and "was part of the 'Georgia Faction'" at the 1809 Huntsville land sale, though "apparently had no political aspirations for himself." Broad River Group leaders (Pope, Bibb, Walker, Tait) founded Huntsville, its bank, and dominated early Alabama politics. JNS Jones was a prominent Huntsville attorney in the same era (1819 Constitutional Convention period), whose law office housed Alabama's first public library. (2026-08-03 update: I ran two independent research passes -- a dedicated Broad River Group research review, and a direct Ancestry profile check of both Llewellen Jones and John N.S. Jones -- and found no documented Georgia [Wilkes/Elbert Co.] residency for either man. Their documented path runs Virginia straight to Alabama, with a Nashville stop for J.N.S. Jones's 1821 marriage. I still have their contemporaneous presence in the same 1809 Huntsville land-sale wave as the Broad River figures documented, but that's the only confirmed connection I've got so far.) I confirmed the Broad River Group is a real, formally named historiographical term, not just a description I made up or that the Huntsville History Collection article implied loosely: it was coined by historian J. Mills Thornton III in his 1978 book 'Politics and Power in a Slave Society: Alabama, 1800-1860' (Louisiana State University Press). The group's origin: in 1784, Gen. George Mathews led Revolutionary War veterans from the Charlottesville, Virginia area to settle along the Broad River in north Georgia, near Petersburg, GA. This group intermarried with existing planter families and became wealthy tobacco/cotton planters, sometimes called the 'Georgia Faction' in Alabama sources -- the exact phrase used in the Huntsville History Collection's Jones-family article. When the federal government opened land around future Huntsville, Broad River investors -- led by LeRoy Pope, John Williams Walker (also a Virginia native, born Amelia County, whose father migrated Amelia Co., VA -> Wilkes Co., GA in 1783), and future governor Thomas Bibb -- bought roughly half the land sold at the 1809 Huntsville public auction. This confirms the Broad River Group is the same migration pattern I've been asking about, and it directly supports treating Llewellen Jones's VA-to-AL migration as historical scaffolding/context, even though I still haven't found a personal or business tie linking him by name to Pope, Bibb, or Walker specifically. [2026-08-04, round 2 targeted follow-up] I did a dedicated follow-up pass this round specifically to check whether our Jones family was really part of the Broad River Group. I confirmed 'Broad River Group' and 'Georgia Faction' are the same historical network -- Chase Tate's Huntsville Historical Review article uses both terms interchangeably (https://huntsvillehistorycollection.org/hhc/docs/pdf/hhr/Volume_39_2_Fall-Winter-14.pdf?a=hhr). But the important nuance: Tate's article names our Llewellen Jones on page 66 ONLY as 'one Huntsville citizen' who hanged himself during the Panic of 1819 -- NOT explicitly as a Broad River Group member. Tate's footnote there cites Daniel Dupre's 'Transforming the Cotton Frontier: Madison County, Alabama, 1800-1840' (LSU Press, 1997), pp.6-7, 57, 62 -- I have NOT examined Dupre's book yet, and it's now my highest-priority unread source (see DB3 new row for Dupre). I also checked E. Merton Coulter's 'Old Petersburg and the Broad River Valley of Georgia' index directly and found ZERO entries for Llewellyn/Lewellen Jones, Spotswood, Perkins, or Scruggs. So Jacquelyn Gray's article remains the ONLY source I've found asserting our Jones family was part of the Broad River Group/Georgia Faction.

It's just a residence listing and doesn't document her relationship to Llewellyn Jones, John Nelson Spotswood Jones, or any specific child. No source is attached to her marriage to Llewellyn Jones or John Nelson Spotswood Jones, and no source is attached to any of the 12 children's relationships to her. The 10 other 'Ancestry Sources' suggestions shown on her profile (Alabama Marriages/Deaths/Wills, Geneanet, Find a Grave, etc.) are all unattached candidate matches, not confirmed sources. Her own birth/death are 'Unknown,' and her listed parents (Judge John Haywood, Martha Edwards) are marked 'Potential father'/'Potential mother' with zero sources.

column10:
This is sensitive historical subject matter (enslaved persons' names, possible enslaver paternity) and I'm writing about it factually and carefully, as an open, unconfirmed hypothesis -- never as settled fact. I'm documenting it because that's the whole point of the Reclaiming Enslaved Names database, not to make a premature identity claim. Cross-reference DB4 row 29 (a related but distinct paternity/tree-conflict question about a different generation) and DB4 row 30 (Shandy's missing tree parent-link, independently established mother via DB2 row 78). [2026-08-04, pass 4 -- STRENGTHENING PRIMARY-SOURCE EVIDENCE] I confirmed directly against the primary source at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (enrolled 1820 legislative act, "An act to authorize John N. S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones to emancipate certain slaves therein named," approved Dec. 11, 1820, ADAH Voices of Alabama collection, item 9761: https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/collection/voices/id/9761/ ; full 2-page zoom viewer: https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/pdf.js/web/viewer.html?file=/digital/api/collection/voices/id/9761/download#page=1&zoom=auto,-96,1269, file ref Q110258-Q110259) that this act is dated December 11, 1820 -- just 9 months after Llewellyn Jones's death on March 6, 1820. Both of his sons, John N.S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones, jointly petitioned to free Elizabeth (40), Evalina (13), Ann (6), and Shandy (3) almost immediately after inheriting/settling their father's estate. This timing is consistent with an inheritance-driven manumission rather than a routine sale-related freeing, which I think meaningfully strengthens this hypothesis. I am NOT treating this as confirmed proof of paternity or of any blood relationship -- the act itself does not state a family relationship between Elizabeth/Evalina/Ann/Shandy and the Jones family, and this remains a strengthened hypothesis only, not a settled fact. This also newly identifies Elizabeth (age 40 in 1820, b. ~1780) as very likely the mother of Evalina/Ann/Shandy per the document's grouping and ages, though the act does not explicitly state that relationship either -- logged as her own entry at DB2 row 76. [2026-08-04, pass 5 -- MY OWN TREE + NAMING-COLLISION CAUTIONS] I went back into my own Ancestry tree ("Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)," Tree ID 210795668) and found that Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell's own tree profile lists her parents as John Nelson Spotswood Jones Esq. (1793-1855) and "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones," and that a woman recorded in my tree as "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" (no birth/death dates given on this particular profile) is listed as spouse/partner of Llewellyn Jones AND as mother of Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell, Paul Llewellyn Jones, Walter Blackstone Jones, John Haywood Jones, Marcella Almira Dearing, Ann Jones (b. 1813), and Elizabeth/Evalina Jones (b. 1807) -- profile https://www.ancestry.com/family-tree/person/tree/210795668/person/302764465198/facts. I want to be very explicit that THIS IS UNVERIFIED TREE DATA FROM MY OWN ANCESTRY TREE, found in my own tree's user-contributed profile fields, NOT a confirmed primary source -- I have not yet opened this specific profile to check what documents (if any) are actually cited for these spousal/parental edges, and it may reflect my own prior guesswork, another user's tree hint, or simple tree conflation/error. I also noticed the tree is internally inconsistent here: one profile lists this Elizabeth's partner as "Llewellyn Jones" while another lists Maria's father as "John Nelson Spotswood Jones Esq." (Llewellyn's son) -- this could mean generational confusion/error in the tree, OR that an Elizabeth was connected to both father and son at different points, OR a plain data-entry mistake. I am flagging this inconsistency, not resolving it. IF accurate, this tree entry would mean Paul Llewellyn Jones, Walter Blackstone Jones, John Haywood Jones, Marcella Almira Dearing, and Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell -- the exact heirs named in the A.P. Jones probate file -- share a mother, an enslaved woman named Elizabeth, with Ann Jones (b.1813) and Elizabeth/Evalina Jones (b.1807), names that closely echo the four people freed in the 1820 emancipation act (Elizabeth 40, Evalina 13, Ann 6, Shandy 3, see row above and DB2 row 76). This could be strong corroborating evidence for this half-sibling hypothesis, OR it could simply be an artifact of tree error/conflation -- I cannot tell which until I check whether these specific tree relationship-edges have actual attached source citations. ACTION ITEM for me, not yet done: open the "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" profile (302764465198) directly and check its source citations before treating any of this as evidence. CAUTION -- NAMING COLLISIONS: I also found that my tree has a SEPARATE "Alexander P Jones" (b. abt. 1795, Virginia - d. Huntsville, Madison Co., AL) whose father is recorded as Turner Moore (1780-1867) -- a completely different lineage from the "Alexander P. Jones" I have been tracking throughout this database as Llewellyn Jones's son and the central figure of the A.P. Jones estate probate. There is also a separate "Alexander Thomas Jones" (1834-1857, son of John N.S. Jones) in the white line. This means there may be TWO OR THREE different "Alexander (P.) Jones" individuals in Madison County across the white slaveholding line and the formerly-enslaved-family line who took the Jones surname -- a real risk of research/logging confusion going forward. I am flagging this prominently so that I (and any future logging pass) do not conflate them. RELATED CAUTION -- THREE DISTINCT ELIZABETHS: my tree also has "Elizabeth Enslaved (1781-1861)," died Huntsville, Madison, AL, partner of Turner Moore, mother of Columbus Jones and this second "Alexander P Jones" -- already logged at DB2 row 185. This is a DIFFERENT woman from the "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" (spouse/partner of Llewellyn/John N.S. Jones, no dates given, profile 302764465198) described earlier in this note, and BOTH are distinct from "Elizabeth" of the 1820 emancipation act (age 40, DB2 row 76, no tree profile). My tree therefore has AT LEAST THREE separate "Elizabeth"s connected to enslavement and the Jones surname. I am tracking these as three distinct individuals pending further verification and will not merge them without direct source evidence.

Jones v. Perkins, 1 Stewart 512-514: Richard Perkins brought trespass to try title in Madison County Circuit Court against Alexander P. Jones for an undivided third of a tract, claiming under a deed from Benjamin Perkins (who claimed a life estate as husband of, and in right of, his wife — a daughter of Lewellen Jones, entitled to one third of his estate). Jones, and Mrs Perkins, the wife of Benjamin Perkins, his heirs at law.' Alexander offered to prove Benjamin's title had vested by sheriff's sale in Thomas Moore, a judgment creditor of Benjamin, before the sale to Richard Perkins — rejected below. Held: reversed and remanded — the defendant, as heir at law (tenant in the nature of a coparcener, not a mere trespasser), could defeat the plaintiff by proving paramount title in a stranger; one tenant in common cannot maintain trespass to try titles against a co-tenant without proving actual ouster. Counsel: Clay and McClung for the plaintiff in error; Kelly and Hutchinson for the defendant. Judge Saffold not sitting; opinion by the Chief Justice. CORRECTION: the opinion does NOT mention the 1820 manumission of Elizabeth or any enslaved person — it is a land-title dispute among Lewellen Jones's heirs. The timeline's characterization of it as 'a case over the title of the 1820 manumission' should be corrected.

Strongest candidate is the 110th USCT (formerly 2nd Alabama Infantry African Descent): organized at Pulaski TN November 20, 1863 for three-year service, designated 110th USCT June 25, 1864, garrisoned at Pulaski and Athens AL guarding North Alabama railroads, mustered out February 6, 1866 (NPS battle-unit detail) — but NO roster match for Columbus Jones found, so this is a contextual lead only, not an identity match. Live alternates: 111th USCT (Pulaski TN January 3, 1864, Athens AL garrison), 12th USCI (recruited Tennessee July–August 1863, three-year term, railroad guard duty, fought at Decatur AL), 57th USCT (organized Decatur AL March 31, 1864). Invalid pension ruled out by chronology — he died in office 1868/1869 and could not have applied himself; a widow’s or minor’s filing is possible but none located in free sources. Death-date conflict: Alabama Mosaic says December 1868, Wikipedia/Foner says 1869 — left Unresolved.

Rowland Jones, usher at the William & Mary grammar school 1700–1702, later burgess for King William County; grandfather (through daughter Frances, m. John Dandridge) of Martha Washington. Rachael (Rachel) Jones, Black freedwoman, Madison County; formerly enslaved by S. Willis Harris; SCC Claim No. 18679, filed Jan 15, 1873. Died March 1875 (per brother David Crow's Aug 26, 1875 deposition).

Claimed $207 (mule, corn, pork); DISALLOWED in full; submitted Sept 9, 1875. Disallowed as one of ten Harris-plantation freedpeople claims, for reasons stated in David Crow No. 18664 (incorporated by reference).

Brother: David Crow (testified 'I am a brother to the claimant in this claim, Rachel Jones').

Husband: Cleiborne (Claiborne) Jones; died in U.S. service, Co. K, 110th U.S. Colored Troops, at Nashville, 1865, in hospital. Married ~1856 (about five years before the war) by their enslaver's consent; 'no license required, only consent of owner.'

Four children (ages Aug 1875): Sarah (~21, oldest), Senia (~16), Thomas (~14), Gable (~12). 'They are the only children they ever had.' No property at either death; no administration; 'This claim is the only effects they had.'

Edward Moore: 'I knew Rachel Jones. We growed up children together. We all belonged to the same owner... I was at the wedding when Claiborn and Rachel was married.' Confirms marriage, children, and that 'Rachel bought the mule' and 'raised them hogs.'

The ten Harris-plantation claimants: Senia McClelland, David Crow, Edward Moore, Stephen Harris, David Vincent, Rachael Jones, Malinda Ellett, Jesse Jefferson, Elizabeth Horton, Benjamin Carter.

Attorneys: Lewis & Fullerton, Washington, D.C.

column2: Did Gross Scruggs Sr. marry 'the widow Jones' after Sept 1832 — and is she Mary Anderson Jones?
column5: Resolved — negative finding: the 'widow Jones' was NOT Mary Anderson Jones. She was MARY SAUNDERS, widow of Major William Jones (1779–1832) of Campbell County, VA — son of William Richard Jones (1745–1781, killed at Guilford Courthouse) and Agness Walker (1749–1798), grandson of John and Elizabeth Walker Jones of Buckingham County, VA; married c.1798/99; seven children survived. After Major Jones's death in 1832 she married Gross Scruggs in Madison County, AL in 1833 — his third wife (after Mary 'Polly' Tate, d. Sept 19, 1832); the Scruggs genealogy also notes she was his fourth marriage's predecessor to 'the widow Shotwell.' Evidence per Ethel Hastings Scruggs Dunklin, The Scruggs Genealogy (1912), via a genealogy.com forum post for John Rison Jones: (1) Gross Scruggs Jr. (b. VA 1796, son of Gross + Nancy Logwood) married Mary Susan Saunders of Tennessee, 'a niece of his step-mother'; (2) Mary Saunders Jones Scruggs d. 1850, will written 1845 witnessed by her nephew William T. Saunders, leaving Saunders silver (6 teaspoons, 6 tablespoons) to son James S. Jones (1800–1853). The Joneses and Scruggses were both Buckingham/Bedford/Campbell VA families, came to Alabama in 1818, and were close neighbors in Madison County. Primary targets: Mary's 1845 will; the Sept 1833 marriage return (Madison Co. Marriage Records v.A — FamilySearch gated).
